metric.why: A facility can have enough total cooling and still starve individual racks; airflow and pressure sensors find recirculation, bypass, and leaks that temperature averages hide.
metric.definition: Cubic feet per minute delivered through the room or containment system, and the pressure differential that drives it through equipment rather than around it.

reading.body:
A data center can deliver enough total cooling capacity while individual racks starve for airflow, making cubic feet per minute and static pressure the real measure of whether equipment gets cooled or recirculation wastes the effort.

Temperature and humidity readings miss the problem because they average across the room. A rack in a recirculation zone or pressure bypass sees hot air cycling back through its inlet, degrading performance or triggering throttling, even when facility-level sensors report normal conditions. Static pressure differential matters because it forces air through the equipment rather than around it. Without pressure tracking, operators see only the symptom, not the cause.

For AI data centers specifically, this gap compounds quickly. GPU clusters generate enormous heat density and have narrow thermal margins. A single rack of high-end accelerators can dissipate hundreds of kilowatts. If airflow bypass or recirculation drops effective cooling by even ten percent, that rack throttles, and throughput drops with it. The facility has paid for the cooling infrastructure; the compute fails anyway because the air never reaches the hardware that needs it.

This metric does not measure total cooling capacity, efficiency, or whether the facility is sized correctly for its workload. It is an operational diagnostic for whether the cooling you built is actually reaching the racks. Temperature sensors alone cannot catch that.
